common.scope: Conceptual model, not an SAP runtime trace.

etag.title: Two readers, one current version
etag.intro: Choose who saves first. Follow the other reader's stale request, refresh and deliberate retry.
etag.initial: Both read quantity 2 with ETag V1.
explanations: Both clients hold the same version. Reading does not reserve the order.
{first} saves quantity {firstQuantity}. V1 matches, so the server writes the change and returns V2.
{second} still sends V1. The server is already at V2 and rejects the write. Quantity {firstQuantity} stays intact.
{second} reads the current quantity {firstQuantity} and V2. Refreshing does not itself save a change.
After reviewing the current data, {second} deliberately chooses quantity {secondQuantity} and saves with V2. The server returns V3; {first}'s local V2 copy is now stale.
etag.takeaway: ETag checks the version sent with a write. A lock coordinates work while held; it is a different mechanism.
etag.limits: This example models ordinary entity ETags. It does not simulate draft locks or total ETag checks. Version labels are illustrative; real ETags are opaque.

tables.title: Choose a table for the access you need
tables.intro: Use the same three orders. Change the table type and task to compare the useful key.
tables.unordered: Cards show membership, not hash order or buckets.
tables.initial: Input order: B/9, A/3, A/5. No secondary keys are defined in this example.
tables.standardAccess: The standard table preserves this insertion order. Without a suitable key, these value searches inspect rows.
tables.sortedFind: The sorted key starts with customer. ID alone is not its leading part, so this search does not get the sorted-key benefit.
tables.sortedCustomer: Customer is the first part of the sorted key. Rows for A form one consecutive key range.
tables.hashedFind: ID is the complete unique hash key. Use that key to locate order 9.
tables.hashedCustomer: Customer is not the hash key. This filter must inspect the rows; hashing ID does not speed up this task.
tables.standardInsert: Insert at the end to preserve input sequence. EMPTY KEY does not enforce unique IDs.
tables.sortedInsert: INSERT INTO TABLE places A/7 after A/5 and before B/9, following the sorted key.
tables.hashedInsert: INSERT INTO TABLE adds ID 7 only if that unique ID is absent. There is no primary index position to choose.
tables.found: One matching row: ID 9, customer B, amount 90.
tables.customerResult: Two matching rows for customer A: IDs 3 and 5.
tables.insertResult: ID 7 was absent. The table now contains four rows.
tables.takeaway: Choose the table and key from real access patterns, not from a claim that one type is always fastest.
tables.limits: The highlight shows logical matches, not measured operations or an exact search algorithm. Memory, row count, secondary keys and update cost also affect the choice.

join.title: Why one order can become two result rows
join.intro: One order is worth 100. It has an English and a German text. Follow the join before adding the amount.
join.empty: Run the join to see its rows.
join.initial: Order 4704 has amount 100. The text key is order + language, so EN and DE are distinct matches.
join.matchingAll: Both texts match order 4704. The join condition does not select one language.
join.matchingOne: Only the {language} text matches both order and language. The other language is excluded.
join.duplicated: The order amount is repeated in two joined rows. The order itself has not been saved twice.
join.single: The joined result has one row, so the amount appears once.
join.sumAll: SUM over these joined rows is 200. The join changed the row count before aggregation.
join.sumOne: SUM over this result is 100. The selected language has exactly one text for this order.
join.takeaway: Check the actual matching rows before aggregating. A cardinality annotation does not remove duplicate matches.
join.limits: This example uses an inner join and a unique text key of order + language. Language filtering alone is not sufficient if the text data can still contain several matches.

http.title: A missing response is not a missing save
http.intro: The server saves a POST, but the response is lost. Compare retrying with and without supported duplicate handling.
http.duplicate: A second record is created in this scenario
explanations: Start a fresh example with zero created records. The request key and payload will stay the same on retry.
The request reaches the server and creates record R1. The client has not yet received the result.
The response is lost after the save. The client sees a timeout; R1 still exists on the server.
http.protectedRetry: The API's documented duplicate-handling contract recognizes K7 with the same payload and returns R1. It does not create a new record.
http.unprotectedRetry: This example endpoint creates R2 on retry because it does not deduplicate. A duplicate is possible, not an inevitable result of every POST API.
http.takeaway: Before retrying a write, check the API's documented retry and duplicate-handling behavior.
http.limits: A made-up header does not create idempotency. Keys, payload comparison, retention and concurrent requests depend on the API contract. This scene models one possible network failure.

grouping.title: One batch, different transaction boundaries
grouping.intro: Run an action for A, B and C. Change B's validity and compare independent changesets with a shared ChangeSet.
grouping.initial: A and C are valid. Each action updates its own order; there are no dependencies or external side effects in this example.
grouping.isolated: Isolated places each invocation in its own changeset. The requests can still travel in one $batch.
grouping.shared: ChangeSet puts these invocations in one atomic changeset. They share the outcome of that group.
grouping.validationInvalid: B fails its business validation. A and C are individually valid, but the group boundary determines what can be saved.
grouping.isolatedFailure: A and C are saved in their own groups. B is rejected; its group is not saved.
grouping.sharedFailure: The shared group fails. None of A, B or C is saved by this changeset.
grouping.success: All three orders are saved. There is no failed validation in this run.
grouping.takeaway: $batch groups transport. A changeset defines the atomic group for these changes.
grouping.limits: This models supported Fiori elements InvocationGrouping. Actual request construction depends on UI5/OData support and the consumer. An action's unrelated remote side effects are not made atomic by this annotation.

dcl.title: Check access where the consumer reads
dcl.intro: Two orders belong to sales organizations A and B. Follow which DCL rule applies at the selected entry point.
dcl.baseIgnored: Base DCL does not automatically carry upward
dcl.initial: The underlying data contains both A/4704 and B/4705. The selected identity is allowed only for {identity}.
dcl.basePath: The consumer reads the base CDS directly. Its active DCL rule applies to this ordinary access.
dcl.exposedPathProtected: The consumer reads the exposed CDS. An explicitly defined equivalent rule protects this entry point.
dcl.exposedPathOpen: The consumer reads the exposed CDS without a DCL rule. Ordinary base-view DCL is not automatically inherited through the view stack.
dcl.filtered: The applicable rule keeps only sales organization {identity}. The other row is filtered out.
dcl.leaked: This unprotected entry returns both organizations in the simplified example. The base DCL alone does not protect it.
dcl.takeaway: Test access through the entity and path the consumer actually uses. Define protection or supported DCL inheritance explicitly.
dcl.limits: This scene assumes ordinary CDS reads, no privileged access, and no other filters or security checks. DCL read access does not replace service access or RAP operation authorization.
